# TimeIndex::host

[Back to TimeIndex API Reference](../../timeindex_api_reference)

## Signature

```cpp
TimeIndex::host() const -> std::vector<std::int64_t>
```

## What It Does

Materializes the time axis as raw epoch-nanosecond ticks on the host.

Use this when you need to hand the timestamps to a lower-level C++ algorithm,
serialize them in your own format, or compare exact machine-time values without
going through text formatting.

This is the machine-facing export, not the human-facing one.

## Returns

`std::vector<std::int64_t>`
    The index values as epoch nanoseconds.

## Examples

Example 1. Export exact machine-time ticks from the index.

```cpp
auto ticks = idx.host();
std::cout << "[";
for (std::size_t i = 0; i < ticks.size(); ++i) {
    if (i != 0) std::cout << ", ";
    std::cout << ticks[i];
}
std::cout << "]\n";
```

### Output

```text
[
  1730419200000000000,
  1730420400000000000,
  1730421600000000000,
  1730422800000000000,
  1730424000000000000
]
```

Example 2. Hand those ticks to a lower-level serializer or C++ kernel.

```cpp
std::vector<std::int64_t> ticks = idx.host();
// write ticks.data() and ticks.size() to your sink
```

## Notes

- `host()` gives exact machine-time values, not formatted strings.
- For human-readable rendering, prefer `idx.timeline().strftime(...)` or
  `idx.timeline().to_note_iso()`.
- The returned values are UTC epoch nanoseconds internally.
- Reach for this when exact comparison or foreign-code interoperability matters
  more than readability.

## See Also

- [`TimeIndex::timeline`](timeline.md): work with the same axis as a `Timeline`.
- [`TimeIndex::size`](size.md): count the number of ticks before exporting.
